title: What are JPA projections (interface, class/DTO, dynamic), and which is most performant?

s1_definition.profdef: JPA projections fetch ONLY the columns you need instead of loading the entire entity. Three forms: (1) INTERFACE-BASED — define an interface with getter methods matching column names; Spring generates a proxy that maps only those columns. `SELECT t.trade_id, t.symbol FROM trades` instead of `SELECT *`. (2) CLASS/DTO — a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new TradeDTO(t.tradeId, t.symbol) FROM Trade t` directly creates DTO instances; or use a record/class as the return type. (3) DYNAMIC — `<T> List<T> findByStatus(String status, Class<T> type)` — the caller chooses the projection at runtime. Performance: DTO projection is MOST performant (no proxy overhead, no entity management, fetches only needed columns). Interface projection adds proxy overhead. Full entity loads all columns + enters persistence context (dirty checking, snapshots).
s1_definition.analogy: Loading the full Trade entity is like requesting the ENTIRE customer file from the vault — 50 pages. Interface projection: "Give me just the name and account number" — 2 fields photocopied onto a slip. DTO projection: "Print a pre-formatted receipt with just name and balance" — direct, no middleman. Dynamic: "Let the customer CHOOSE what they want to see" — flexible.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface = proxy with getter methods. DTO = constructor expression or record return (fastest — no proxy, no entity management). Dynamic = Class<T> parameter, caller picks. Always prefer DTO for API responses — fetches only what's needed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JPA projections fetch ONLY the columns you need instead of loading the entire entity. Three forms: (1) INTERFACE-BASED — define an interface with getter methods matching column names; Spring generates a proxy that maps only those columns. `SELECT t.trade_id, t.symbol FROM trades` instead of `SELECT *`. (2) CLASS/DTO — a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new TradeDTO(t.tradeId, t.symbol) FROM Trade t` directly creates DTO instances; or use a record/class as the return type. (3) DYNAMIC — `<T> List<T> findByStatus(String status, Class<T> type)` — the caller chooses the projection at runtime. Performance: DTO projection is MOST performant (no proxy overhead, no entity management, fetches only needed columns). Interface projection adds proxy overhead. Full entity loads all columns + enters persistence context (dirty checking, snapshots).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Loading the full Trade entity is like requesting the ENTIRE customer file from the vault — 50 pages. Interface projection: "Give me just the name and account number" — 2 fields photocopied onto a slip. DTO projection: "Print a pre-formatted receipt with just name and balance" — direct, no middleman. Dynamic: "Let the customer CHOOSE what they want to see" — flexible.

**One line to remember:** Interface = proxy with getter methods. DTO = constructor expression or record return (fastest — no proxy, no entity management). Dynamic = Class<T> parameter, caller picks. Always prefer DTO for API responses — fetches only what's needed.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's trade listing API returns trade data to the frontend.** The Trade entity has 15 columns including large TEXT fields (notes, audit_trail). The frontend only needs tradeId, symbol, and amount for the list view. Loading full entities fetches 15 columns × 50,000 trades = massive data transfer, plus Hibernate manages all 50,000 in the persistence context (memory + dirty checking). The team creates three projections: interface for quick prototyping, DTO record for the production API (fastest), and dynamic projection for the flexible search endpoint where the caller chooses the detail level.

**What the project will show:** Interface projection (2 fields), DTO/record projection with JPQL constructor (3 fields — fastest), dynamic projection with Class<T> parameter, full entity for comparison, and performance logging showing column count and persistence context size differences.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Full entity.** `SELECT * FROM trades WHERE status = 'SETTLED'`. All 12 columns loaded including TEXT fields (notes, audit_trail). Each entity enters persistence context — snapshot stored for dirty checking. Memory: 50K entities × 12 fields × 2 (entity + snapshot) = heavy.

**Step 2 — Interface projection.** `SELECT trade_id, symbol FROM trades WHERE status = 'SETTLED'`. Only 2 columns fetched. Spring creates proxy objects implementing TradeIdAndSymbol. Proxies map getTradeId() → trade_id column, getSymbol() → symbol column. NO persistence context entry. Memory: 50K × 2 fields = light.

**Step 3 — DTO projection.** `SELECT trade_id, symbol, amount FROM trades WHERE status = 'SETTLED'`. Only 3 columns. Hibernate calls `new TradeOverview(tradeId, symbol, amount)` for each row. Plain record objects — no proxy overhead. NO persistence context. Memory: lightest.

**Step 4 — Dynamic.** `findByAccountId("SAV2001", TradeOverview.class)`. Spring detects TradeOverview is NOT an entity → uses DTO projection. Same SQL as DTO approach. Caller can also pass `Trade.class` to get full entities from the same method.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREE PROJECTION TYPES ═══

  FULL ENTITY:
    SELECT * FROM trades (12 columns)
    → Trade entity → persistence context (dirty checking, snapshots)
    →  MOST memory,  SLOWEST

  INTERFACE PROJECTION:
    SELECT trade_id, symbol FROM trades (2 columns)
    → Spring proxy implementing TradeIdAndSymbol
    →  Less memory, proxy overhead

  DTO/RECORD PROJECTION:
    SELECT trade_id, symbol, amount FROM trades (3 columns)
    → new TradeOverview(tradeId, symbol, amount) — plain object
    →  LEAST memory, FASTEST (no proxy, no persistence context)

  DYNAMIC PROJECTION:
    <T> List<T> findByAccountId(id, Class<T> type)
    → type = TradeOverview.class → DTO projection
    → type = TradeIdAndSymbol.class → Interface projection
    → type = Trade.class → Full entity

  ═══ PERFORMANCE RANKING ═══
  1. DTO record     ← FASTEST (3 columns, plain object, no PC)
  2. Interface       ← FAST (2 columns, proxy overhead)
  3. Full entity    ← SLOWEST (12 columns, persistence context)
```

```
  Projections fetch a subset of columns → less I/O, no persistence-context tracking.
  Interface = proxy over selected getters; DTO = JPQL "new" constructor expression.
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Projection Forms & Tradeoffs (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DTO Pattern: thin, immutable read model                          │
  │  Strategy: interface vs DTO vs dynamic selection per query         │

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> AccountSummary (interface proj.)  │
  │  getId():Long  getBalance():BigDecimal          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ record AccountDto(Long id,BigDecimal balance)   │ (constructor proj.)
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  │ <<interface>> AccountRepository                 │
  │  List<AccountSummary> findByStatus(String s);   │
  │  @Query("select new ...AccountDto(a.id,         │
  │     a.balance) from Account a where a.branch=:b")│
  │  List<AccountDto> dtoByBranch(String b);        │

  Rule: prefer flat projections; choose DTO when you need explicit mapping/compute.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA projections fetch only the columns you need instead of loading the full entity. Three forms: interface-based defines an interface with getter methods — Spring generates a proxy mapping only those columns. DTO/class-based uses a JPQL constructor expression or a record return type — creates plain objects with no proxy and no persistence context entry. Dynamic projection accepts `Class<T>` as a parameter, letting the caller choose the projection at runtime. Performance ranking: DTO is fastest (fewest columns, no proxy overhead, no persistence context management), interface is second (few columns but proxy creation cost), full entity is slowest (all columns, snapshot storage, dirty checking).

In my trade listing service, the Trade entity has 12 columns including large TEXT fields. The list view needs only tradeId, symbol, and amount. DTO projection `TradeOverview(tradeId, symbol, amount)` fetches 3 columns instead of 12 — 75% less data transferred. With 50,000 trades: full entity loads 600,000 field values + 50,000 snapshots. DTO loads 150,000 field values, zero snapshots. The SQL clearly shows the difference: `SELECT trade_id, symbol, amount` vs `SELECT *`.

Always prefer DTO projections for REST API responses — they fetch exactly what the frontend needs, avoid over-fetching, reduce memory, skip persistence context overhead, and produce lightweight response payloads. Use interface projections for quick prototyping or when you need Spring's proxy features (like computed values via SpEL in `@Value` annotations on the interface). Use full entities only when you need to MODIFY the data (dirty checking requires the full entity in the persistence context).
